newsitem.title: UK: Britain denies negotiating terms for IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Britain denies negotiating terms for IRA ceasefire.

text.p: The British government denied on Sunday that it was negotiating terms of a new IRA ceasefire with Gerry Adams, head of the guerrillas' political wing, Sinn Fein.

A spokesman for Britain's Northern Ireland Office (NIO) said the government had no contact with Sinn Fein and dismissed a report in the Sunday Tribune newspaper that it was discussing a new IRA truce using Irish nationalist John Hume as a go-between.

But Hume, leader of the Social, Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP), confirmed that he was involved in talks on a new IRA truce with Adams and was keeping the British and Irish governments, sponsors of Northern Ireland peace talks, informed. "I have been saying for some time that I have maintained contact with Gerry Adams with the objective of restoring the ceasefire," Hume told reporters.
"I have been saying that publicly. You can take it for granted that if I am trying to restore a ceasefire I am keeping both governments informed of what I am doing," Hume said.

Adams, shunned by both Britain and Ireland since the Irish Republican Army broke a 17-month ceasefire in February, echoed Hume's statement. "John Hume and I haven't stopped working. We continue to work. We have been closely focused since the peace process collapse to create the conditions for it to be restored and the restoration of proper talks aimed at bringing about agreement and a negotiated settlement," he said.

The Sunday Tribune, which gave no source for its report, said Hume was carrying drafts of terms for a new IRA ceasefire to admit Sinn Fein to the talks, which involve every other political party in the province.
The report was published days after Irish Prime Minister John Bruton told parliament he believed a new IRA ceasefire was imminent but gave no reason for his optimism.

The IRA resumed its war against British rule of the province in February with attacks on Britain, a British army base in Germany and a twin car-bomb assault at Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters outside Belfast on October 7.
That attack was the first by the IRA in the province for two years and raised fears that it would spark retaliation by Protestant Loyalists, who have to date maintained their own two-year-old truce.

The British and Irish governments say that the IRA must restore its ceasefire to join the talks but Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Sir Patrick Mayhew, has said London wants proof that the ceasefire is genuine, not tactical.
The NIO spokesman said a ceasefire would not automatically gain Sinn Fein entry to the peace talks.
"As we have said many times after the murderous attacks we have seen, there could be no question of the IRA declaring a ceasefire one day and Sinn Fein joining the talks the next."
The IRA ended its truce accusing Britain of making the surrender of its guerrilla arsenals a precondition for Sinn Fein's entry to the peace talks.
Britain has changed its attitude on the so-called decommissioning of weapons since the ending of the IRA truce and now says that Sinn Fein must discuss it at some stage in the peace talks.
But Sinn Fein and the IRA say that the surrender of weapons must wait until a final settlement is agreed to end a 27-year conflict which killed 3,200.
